key_concept: The endomembrane system is the group of membrane-bound organelles whose functions are coordinated: ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles; mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are excluded because their functions are not coordinated with these.
steps: Recall the definition: organelles whose functions are coordinated form the endomembrane system. These are the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles.
The coordination works as a flow of material. Proteins and lipids are made in the ER and modified and packaged in the Golgi. Golgi vesicles then form lysosomes and contribute to vacuoles.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts are excluded. They are semi-autonomous, with their own DNA and $70S$ ribosomes, and their functions are not coordinated with the ER–Golgi pathway.
Peroxisomes are excluded too, because they are not part of this coordinated ER–Golgi–lysosome pathway.
Check each option. Options (2), (3) and (4) all contain chloroplast and/or peroxisomes (option (3) also has mitochondria), so they are wrong.
Only option (1) lists all four members: ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuole.
final_answer: Option (1): endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuole
why_not_others: Options (2), (3) and (4) each include chloroplast and peroxisomes (and option (3) also includes mitochondria). These organelles work independently and are not part of the coordinated endomembrane system, even though they are membrane-bound.
common_trap: Students assume that every membrane-bound organelle belongs to the endomembrane system and wrongly include mitochondria, chloroplasts or peroxisomes.
time_saving_tip: Eliminate any option containing mitochondria, chloroplast or peroxisome; only option (1) survives.
